prompt.context_jp: 夜の街角に、ATMの青白い光___ぽつんと浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 夜の街角に、ATMの青白い光___ぽつんと浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces the ATM's pale light as a new scene element.

feedback.correct_en: The opening sentence introduces the ATM's light as fresh scene information — が marks newly-presented subjects in a descriptive setting.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the light as an already-known topic, which doesn't fit a scene-opening description. を would be ungrammatical with 浮かんでいた (an intransitive state).

contrast_examples.en: A mountain is visible over there. (new info — が)
That mountain is Mt. Fuji. (known topic — は)

prompt.context_jp: お金の流れ___、ときに持ち主の言葉よりも正直に、その人の素顔を語る。
prompt.prompt_jp: お金の流れ___、ときに持ち主の言葉よりも正直に、その人の素顔を語る。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that sets up 'the flow of money' as the general topic of commentary.

feedback.correct_en: This is a generalizing statement about what 'the flow of money' does — は establishes it as the topic being characterized.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present it as new/identifying information, but the sentence is a reflective generalization, not an event. を doesn't fit — 流れ is the subject that 'speaks', not an object.

contrast_examples.en: Oh, there's a cat. (new info — が)

prompt.context_jp: フロアには、キーボードを打つ乾いた音だけ___響いている。
prompt.prompt_jp: フロアには、キーボードを打つ乾いた音だけ___響いている。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits with だけ to exhaustively identify the only sound in the room.

feedback.correct_en: 〜だけが with an existence/perception verb exhaustively identifies 'the one thing' present. The scene emphasizes that nothing else can be heard.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would weaken the exhaustive 'only this' nuance and sound contrastive instead. に would mark a location, not the subject that is sounding.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は知っているが、他は知らない。
contrast_examples.en: He knows, but others don't. (contrastive は)

prompt.context_jp: 「“川島ゆり子” これ___沙羅さんの本名か」
prompt.prompt_jp: これ___沙羅さんの本名か
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle: Souma has just seen the real name and is identifying it as such.

feedback.correct_en: 'これが本名か' — が highlights the identification: 'So *this* is the real name.' It picks the newly-revealed name out as the answer.
feedback.incorrect_en: 'これは本名か' would sound like a flat yes/no question about whether it is her real name, rather than the exclamatory recognition the moment calls for.

prompt.context_jp: 最初にそれに気づいたの___、相馬の鋭い目だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 最初にそれに気づいたの___、相馬の鋭い目だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for a cleft-like sentence specifying who noticed first.

feedback.correct_en: In the 〜のは〜だった cleft pattern, は marks the presupposed part ('the one who noticed first') and the predicate identifies who it was.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would break the cleft structure — the known/presupposed clause takes は, with new identifying info coming after だった.

contrast_examples.jp: 優勝したのは田中さんだ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who won is Tanaka. (cleft — のは)

prompt.context_jp: 支店にとってなじみのある名前___、思いもよらない場所に現れたのだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 支店にとってなじみのある名前___、思いもよらない場所に現れたのだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle: the sentence reveals a surprising event — a familiar name appearing where it shouldn't.

feedback.correct_en: が presents the subject as part of newly-noticed/eventive information — the dramatic revelation that this familiar name has turned up unexpectedly.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame '名前' as an already-set topic being described, which deflates the surprise. The のだ ending here delivers a discovery.

contrast_examples.jp: 知らない人が入ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: An unknown person came in. (new event — が)

contrast_examples.jp: その人はよく来る客だ。
contrast_examples.en: That person is a regular. (known topic — は)

prompt.context_jp: 顧客の信用情報を外に持ち出し、それを失ってしまったのは、確かに彼自身の落ち度___。
prompt.prompt_jp: ...失ってしまったの___、確かに彼自身の落ち度だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for the 〜のは〜だった cleft identifying whose fault it was.

feedback.correct_en: The cleft structure 〜のは…だった marks the presupposition with は; the identified answer ('his own fault') follows.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would break the cleft; the presupposed clause 'losing it' is the topic being commented on.

contrast_examples.jp: 遅れたのは私のせいだ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who was late — it's my fault. (のは cleft)

prompt.context_jp: 「私は 松木さんみたいに 真面目で まっすぐな人こそ 銀行には必要だと思います」
prompt.prompt_jp: 松木さんみたいに真面目でまっすぐな人こそ銀行には必要だ
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle on 私 at the start — '私は...思います' — fits Mai asserting her personal view?

feedback.correct_en: When stating one's own opinion/belief with と思います, 私は frames 'as for me, I think...' as the speaker's standpoint.
feedback.incorrect_en: 私が would spotlight 'I (and no one else) think' — exhaustive and assertive in a way that sounds confrontational here. Mai is sharing, not insisting she's the only believer.

contrast_examples.en: I'll do it (I'm the one). (exhaustive — が)

prompt.context_jp: 処分を覚悟しているはずなのに、彼の目___数字と文字から一瞬も離れない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 処分を覚悟しているはずなのに、彼の目___数字と文字から一瞬も離れない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits the contrastive 'and yet his eyes...' feel.

feedback.correct_en: のに sets up a contrast; は on 彼の目 highlights the subject as the thing being contrasted ('despite that, HIS eyes don't leave the page').
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just report a neutral event, losing the contrastive weight that のに demands.

contrast_examples.jp: 疲れているのに、彼は休まない。
contrast_examples.en: Even though he's tired, he doesn't rest. (contrast — は)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が休まないから心配だ。
contrast_examples.en: I worry because he won't rest. (neutral subject — が)

prompt.context_jp: 表に立たされているの___沙羅で、糸を引いている本人___安全な場所から動かない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 表に立たされているのは沙羅で、糸を引いている本人___安全な場所から動かない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle: the sentence contrasts Sara (out front) with the mastermind (hiding safely).

feedback.correct_en: This is explicit contrast: Sara vs. the one pulling strings. Contrastive は pairs the two clauses against each other.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just introduce a new subject neutrally, losing the pointed comparison between the two parties.

contrast_examples.jp: 兄は背が高いが、弟は低い。
contrast_examples.en: The older brother is tall, but the younger is short. (contrast — は)
The little brother is crying. (new info — が)

prompt.context_jp: やがて約束の時刻ちょうどに、一人の女性___ロビーに姿を現した。
prompt.prompt_jp: やがて約束の時刻ちょうどに、一人の女性___ロビーに姿を現した。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces a new character stepping into the scene.

feedback.correct_en: 一人の女性 is brand-new in the narrative — が introduces newly-appearing characters/entities in descriptive narration.
feedback.incorrect_en: は presupposes the woman is already a known topic, which doesn't match 'a certain woman appeared.'

contrast_examples.jp: その男はスパイだった。
contrast_examples.en: That man was a spy. (known topic — は)

prompt.context_jp: 「そのお金___持っていったら あなた方を 告訴しなければなりません」
prompt.prompt_jp: そのお金___持っていったら、あなた方を告訴しなければなりません
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle marking the direct object of 持っていく.

feedback.correct_en: 持っていく takes a direct object marked by を — the money is what gets carried off.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the money the subject, but 持っていく needs an agent (Sara) and object (the money). は is possible but would topicalize contrastively; を is the direct, neutral choice.

contrast_examples.en: I'll take the bag. (direct object — を)

prompt.context_jp: 「そもそも 悪いの___銀行じゃないか」
prompt.prompt_jp: そもそも悪いの___銀行じゃないか
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for the cleft 'the one who's bad is the bank, isn't it?'

feedback.correct_en: 〜のは〜じゃないか is a cleft blaming structure: は marks the presupposed 'the bad one', with the identification following.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would break the cleft; Kasai is pointing at who among candidates is to blame, which calls for the のは cleft frame.

contrast_examples.en: The one at fault is you. (のは cleft)

prompt.context_jp: 「悪いのは 全部 こいつだよ！ 俺___悪くない！」
prompt.prompt_jp: 俺___悪くない！
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle: Kasai is contrastively insisting *he's* not the bad one — someone else is.

feedback.correct_en: Contrastive は: 'As for me, I'm not at fault' — explicitly contrasting himself with Sara, whom he just blamed.
feedback.incorrect_en: 俺が悪くない would sound unnatural here; the discourse is a defensive contrast ('*that guy* is bad, *I'm* not'), which is exactly what contrastive は expresses.

prompt.context_jp: 「あなた___経営者として 間違ってます！」
prompt.prompt_jp: あなた___経営者として間違ってます！
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle: Mai is directly characterizing Kasai as the topic of her accusation.

feedback.correct_en: は takes 'you' as the topic and delivers a judgment about him: 'As a business owner, you are wrong.' This is a characterization, not an identification.
feedback.incorrect_en: あなたが間違ってます would sound like picking him out from a group ('you're the one who's wrong, not someone else') — the force here is characterizing him, which uses は.

prompt.context_jp: 「今 もう1人 ものすごく苦しんでる人___います 松木さんです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 今もう1人、ものすごく苦しんでる人___います
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle introducing a new person Mai wants Kasai to notice.

feedback.correct_en: います/あります with an indefinite noun ('one more person') introduces something new — が is the standard existential-presentation particle.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose this person is already a known topic, but Mai is bringing Matsuki into the conversation for the first time here.

contrast_examples.jp: もう一人お客さんがいる。

contrast_examples.en: That person is a customer. (known topic — は)

prompt.context_jp: 「2年前に この支店で 口座を___しています」
prompt.prompt_jp: 2年前にこの支店で口座を___しています
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb that collocates with 口座を for 'opening an account.'

feedback.correct_en: 口座を開設する is the fixed banking expression for opening an account.
feedback.incorrect_en: 開放 means 'to open up / release' (as of a facility to the public). 開催 means 'to host an event.' Neither collocates with 口座.

contrast_examples.jp: 新しい口座を開設する。

prompt.context_jp: 「___野郎だ！ おい 松木 何してる！」
prompt.prompt_jp: ___野郎だ！
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the expression that fits Souma's outraged outburst about Kasai.

feedback.correct_en: とんでもない野郎 = 'what an outrageous bastard.' Pure moral indignation — fits Souma's reaction to Kasai's extortion scheme.
feedback.incorrect_en: もったいない means 'a waste.' つまらない means 'boring/trivial.' Neither captures the anger at a terrible person.

prompt.context_jp: 松木の顔から、さっと___が引いていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 松木の顔から、さっと___が引いていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that completes the idiom for color draining from someone's face.

feedback.correct_en: 顔から血の気が引く is the set idiom for turning pale from shock/fear. It describes Matsuki's horrified reaction to the revelation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 息が引く isn't idiomatic. 元気が引く doesn't exist as a set phrase — one would say 元気がなくなる.

contrast_examples.en: The color drained from my face.

prompt.context_jp: 証拠もないまま相手を問い詰めれば、かえって___をすくわれかねない。
prompt.prompt_jp: かえって___をすくわれかねない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the body part completing the idiom for 'being tripped up / caught off guard.'

feedback.correct_en: 足元をすくわれる — 'to have one's feet swept out' — is the idiom for being outmaneuvered or caught in a weakness.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手をすくわれる / 頭をすくわれる aren't idiomatic. The image is specifically of losing one's footing.

contrast_examples.jp: 油断すると足元をすくわれる。
contrast_examples.en: Let your guard down and you'll be tripped up.

prompt.context_jp: 「追加融資の___を書いてるんですか？」
prompt.prompt_jp: 追加融資の___を書いてるんですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word for the internal proposal document a loan officer writes.

feedback.correct_en: 稟議書 is the specific internal approval document in Japanese banking/corporate practice — exactly what a loan officer drafts to get a loan approved.
feedback.incorrect_en: 領収書 is a receipt. 企画書 is a project proposal (used for marketing/business planning, not loan approval).

prompt.context_jp: 待ちきれなくなった葛西は、___を切らしてロビーへと足を踏み入れた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___を切らしてロビーへと足を踏み入れた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that completes the idiom for 'losing patience.'

feedback.correct_en: しびれを切らす is the fixed idiom for 'running out of patience' — literally 'to let numbness run out.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 息を切らす means 'to be out of breath' (physical). 気を切らす isn't a set idiom.

contrast_examples.jp: しびれを切らして出て行った。

prompt.context_jp: 「今回の一連の行為は 明らかに___に当たるらしい」
prompt.prompt_jp: 今回の一連の行為は明らかに___に当たるらしい
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the legal term for forcing someone to pay by threat.

feedback.correct_en: 恐喝 (extortion) — using threats to extract money — is exactly what Kasai did by using the stolen file as leverage for a 'reward.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 詐欺 is fraud (deception, not threat). 窃盗 is theft; stealing the file was theft, but the 'series of actions' including the demand is specifically extortion.

prompt.context_jp: 「葛西社長が___だと 証明するためには…」
prompt.prompt_jp: 葛西社長が___だと証明するためには
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word for 'mastermind / person pulling the strings behind the scenes.'

feedback.correct_en: 黒幕 is the behind-the-scenes schemer — fits Kasai, who stayed hidden while Sara did the dirty work.
feedback.incorrect_en: 主役 is 'lead role' (neutral/positive). 犯人 just means 'the perpetrator' — true but doesn't convey the 'hidden manipulator' nuance Souma emphasizes.

contrast_examples.en: Expose the mastermind behind the incident.

prompt.context_jp: Scene: Mai heads immediately to Sawada Construction after the meeting.
prompt.prompt_jp: Which phrasing sounds most natural in narrative prose?
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the most natural narrative sentence.

choices.text: 舞はその足で、下町の一角にあるサワダ建業に赴いた。
舞はその足で、サワダ建業に下町の一角にある赴いた。
舞がその足で、下町の一角にあるサワダ建業に赴いた。

feedback.correct_en: The relative clause 下町の一角にある correctly precedes the noun サワダ建業 it modifies, and the topic は places Mai as the ongoing subject of the paragraph.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B scrambles the relative clause so it no longer modifies anything coherently. Option C uses が, which would spotlight Mai as new info — but she's the established protagonist, so は fits.

contrast_examples.jp: 駅前にあるカフェに行った。
contrast_examples.en: I went to the café in front of the station. (natural order)

contrast_examples.jp: カフェに駅前にある行った。

prompt.context_jp: Scene: Mai tells Souma she's going to visit the anxious client, Sawada.
prompt.prompt_jp: Which version of 'I'll go tell them quickly' sounds most natural for Mai speaking to her senior?
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the most natural phrasing.

feedback.correct_en: 〜てきます (polite 〜ます + 'go do and come back') is the right register for Mai talking to Souma — professional but not overly formal.
feedback.incorrect_en: B drops to plain form, too casual for workplace use with a senior. C uses humble 参ります, which is excessive here (used for superiors/customers, not peers like Souma).

contrast_examples.en: I'll go buy it and come back. (polite, standard)
I shall go purchase it. (very humble, for customers)

prompt.context_jp: Scene: Mai angrily protests that hardworking people lose out while cheaters benefit.
prompt.prompt_jp: Which sounds most natural for 'hardworking people suffer / are made fools of'?
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the most natural idiomatic phrasing.

choices.text: 一生懸命やっている人がバカを見るなんておかしいです。
一生懸命やっている人がバカを作るなんておかしいです。
一生懸命やっている人にバカが見えるなんておかしいです。

feedback.correct_en: バカを見る is the set idiom for 'to get the short end of the stick / be made a fool of despite effort.' It's exactly Mai's point.
feedback.incorrect_en: バカを作る (B) isn't an idiom — 'to make a fool' would be バカにする. Option C literally means 'a fool becomes visible to them,' which is nonsense.

contrast_examples.en: The honest person gets the short end.
Don't make a fool of people.

prompt.context_jp: Scene: Matsuki, nervous, asks Mai out before boarding the Shinkansen.
prompt.prompt_jp: Which phrasing feels most natural for a shy, warm invitation between coworkers?
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the most natural variant.

choices.text: 何かおいしいものを食べに行きませんか？
何かおいしいものを食べに行きますか？
何かおいしいものを食べに行くか？

feedback.correct_en: 〜ませんか？ is the standard polite invitation — soft, inviting, perfect for a hesitant 'won't you join me?'
feedback.incorrect_en: B (行きますか) is a flat yes/no question about intent, not an invitation. C is blunt masculine casual, inappropriate for Matsuki's shy, polite personality here.

contrast_examples.jp: お茶を飲みに行きませんか？
お茶を飲みに行きますか？
contrast_examples.en: Are you going for tea? (plain question)

prompt.context_jp: Scene: The branch manager thanks the woman as she hands back the file.
prompt.prompt_jp: Which phrasing sounds most natural for a branch manager politely thanking someone in a formal setting?
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the most natural polite phrasing.

choices.text: 大切なものを届けていただきありがとうございます。
大切なものを届けてくれてありがとう。
大切なものを届けさせてくださりありがとうございます。

feedback.correct_en: 〜ていただき is the humble form that correctly thanks a customer for an action they performed for the speaker's side — standard business politeness.
feedback.incorrect_en: B (〜てくれてありがとう) is casual, inappropriate for a branch manager addressing an outsider. C misuses 〜させてくださり (causative-passive honorific), which would mean 'thank you for letting me deliver,' the opposite direction.

contrast_examples.jp: ご来店いただきありがとうございます。
contrast_examples.en: Thank you for visiting our store. (business)

contrast_examples.jp: 来てくれてありがとう。
